CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left ankle pain

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male who sustained an injury to his left ankle yesterday while on a walk with his wife. He stepped off a curb and landed on the ankle incorrectly. Denies hearing a pop but describes feeling the ankle stretched and extended. He reports pain on the outside of the ankle that has been present for a couple of days. Patient was able to ambulate back to his house after the injury, though it was painful. He has attempted home management with ibuprofen, elevation, ice, and weight-bearing avoidance. Pain is rated 8/10 without medication and improves to approximately 7/10 with ibuprofen. Denies any substantial previous injuries to this ankle.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient reports pain and swelling in the left ankle. Vitals noted to be stable but slightly elevated, likely related to pain.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant past medical history. Denies substantial previous ankle injuries.

MEDICATIONS
Ibuprofen
Acetaminophen

ALLERGIES
Not documented

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented

SOCIAL HISTORY
Married. Takes regular walks, particularly since working from home during COVID-19 pandemic.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Stable, slightly elevated
Left ankle: Ecchymosis and bruising over the lateral malleolus with swelling and edema noted. Positive for tenderness to palpation on the lateral side with soft tissue swelling. No laxity appreciated in the joint. No bony tenderness to palpation of the foot.
Neurovascular exam of left foot: Capillary refill brisk (less than 3 seconds). Strong dorsalis pedis pulses bilaterally. Motor and sensory function intact and symmetric bilaterally.

RESULTS
X-ray of left ankle: No fracture or bony abnormalities identified.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Left ankle sprain of the lateral ligament complex. The lateral ligament on the outside of the ankle was stretched with the fall. Patient to continue RICE protocol (rest, ice, compression, elevation). Air cast provided for ankle stabilization. Crutches prescribed with instruction to stay off the leg but begin walking as tolerated over the next several days. Continue NSAIDs to reduce pain and swelling. Symptoms expected to improve significantly over 4-7 days. Follow-up appointment scheduled in 2 weeks. Patient instructed to return if symptoms worsen or if pain becomes severe.
